name: Payment System
strapline: Idempotent Go payment lifecycle: order, charge, HMAC callbacks, outbox, refunds.
why: Payment retries are where systems go wrong: a customer double-clicks, a partner callback arrives twice, a worker dies mid-flight. This repo keeps those paths in one place - a single TransactionLifecycle module that pairs the PostgreSQL transaction, the outbox row and the idempotency key - so there is exactly one way a payment changes state.

It was written as a reference implementation rather than a product: the unglamorous half of payments as code you can start with docker compose, break on purpose and read. HMAC-verified callbacks with a replay window, an outbox poller that ends poison messages in a DLQ, and a sweeper that keeps stale state honest.
what: A working payment lifecycle built end to end: a customer signs in, picks a product, places an order, charges it, and refunds it. Every state change runs through one TransactionLifecycle module that pairs a PostgreSQL transaction with an outbox row and an idempotency key, so retries and duplicate clicks cannot double-charge.

It exists as a reference implementation of the unglamorous parts of payments: HMAC-verified partner callbacks with a 300s replay window, background workers that turn outbox rows into invoice files, and a dead-letter queue for poison messages.
It is aimed at backend engineers who want to read real code for retries, callbacks and reconciliation rather than a slide deck about them.

stack.name: Go
stack.role: The whole backend is one binary. Lifecycle, store and jobs are plain Go over database/sql with no ORM, so the transaction boundary and the idempotency insert stay visible in one function.

stack.name: PostgreSQL
stack.role: System of record for the transaction and store schemas: one SQL transaction writes the state change, the outbox row and the idempotency key, which is what makes retries safe.

stack.name: Redis
stack.role: Short-lived charge state for the partner stub (ms-paymentagr), so the fake provider can behave like one without a database of its own.

stack.name: Next.js 16 + TypeScript + Tailwind
stack.role: The portal - login, catalog, checkout, status, refunds. Its server-side client (frontend/src/lib/gateway.ts) calls the monolith, so browser code never holds a partner key.

stack.name: Docker Compose
stack.role: Five containers (postgres, redis, ms-paymentagr, monolith, frontend) from one command; pg-init-scripts seed schemas, demo users and products, so the lifecycle is runnable with no cloud account.

structure: monolith/lifecycle/ - the deep module: lifecycle.go holds the state chart (CREATED to READY to SUCCESS/FAILED/REFUND) plus idempotency, and pricing.go holds the discount math.
monolith/cmd/ - wiring and the endpoint table: routes.go, handlers.go for the new API, legacy.go for the ms-* compatible paths, http.go for envelopes plus partner and outbox transport.
monolith/store/ - the persistence seam: store.go types with pg.go for production and memory.go as the dev/test fake, over the transaction + store schemas.
monolith/jobs/, monolith/invoice/, monolith/invoiceworker/ - the background half: the outbox poller, the sweeper and the invoice worker that writes receipt files.
ms-paymentagr/ - the partner stub (Go/Gin + Redis): usecase/ drives charge, refund, the CheckoutUrl page and HMAC-SHA256 callbacks behind the api-key header.
frontend/ - the Next.js portal; frontend/src/lib/gateway.ts is the only place that talks to the monolith.
architecture: State only changes through the lifecycle module: the state change, the outbox row and the idempotency key are written in one PostgreSQL transaction, so a repeat of the same Idempotency-Key returns the original result instead of charging twice.
Callbacks are verified before they are trusted: HMAC-SHA256 over the body with a 300s replay window; a forged signature is rejected with 401 and never reaches the lifecycle.

Asynchronous work is a table, not a queue client: outbox.go polls every 5s, routes ms-notify-payment rows to the invoice worker and keeps servicelogs queryable, retries with 3x backoff and terminates poison messages in a dlq.* row.
The sweeper keeps stale state honest: READY transactions older than 5m move to FAILED, and servicelogs are purged past LOG_RETENTION_DAYS.
The invoice worker writes INVOICE_DIR/invoice_<tx>.json and sanitizes the transaction id against path traversal before it touches the filesystem.

The README publishes no benchmark numbers: splitting the monolith is explicitly deferred until a load measurement justifies it, which is why this repo shows a lifecycle rather than a throughput claim.
install: # edit .env and set every secret (PARTNER_API_KEY, NOTIFY_SECRET, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, ...)
quickstart: Wait for the five containers (postgres, redis, ms-paymentagr, monolith, frontend) to go healthy; the first boot seeds the schemas, outbox/idempotency tables and demo users/products.
Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with one of the seeded demo accounts from project/pg-init-scripts/sql/20-store-schema.sql.
Place an order and watch the state move: POST /ms/api/v1/order/product with an Idempotency-Key inserts product_trx as CREATED plus its outbox and idempotency rows in one transaction.
Create the payment: POST /ms/api/v1/payment/create/SHOPEEPAY?transaction_id= moves CREATED to READY and returns a CheckoutUrl; calling it twice returns the same url.

A signed SUCCEEDED callback to POST /ms/api/v1/payment/notify (with x-callback-signature and x-callback-timestamp) drives READY to SUCCESS, and within 5s the poller writes INVOICE_DIR/invoice_<tx>.json; a forged signature is rejected with 401.
Refund with POST /ms/api/v1/payment/refund (SUCCESS to REFUND) - a second refund returns 409 - then read the audit trail at GET /v1/logs?limit=.
tradeoffs: The README publishes no benchmark numbers: the service-split decision is explicitly deferred until a load measurement justifies it, so there is no latency or throughput evidence to quote.
Callback verification is wide open when NOTIFY_SECRET is unset - the README documents that as a local-dev-only state, not a deployable one.
Sessions are short-lived opaque tokens held in memory, so they do not survive a restart or span instances.

The Java/Spring services are decommissioned and no longer in the tree - only the Go monolith, the partner stub and the Next.js frontend ship, with git history (and one leftover diagram) preserving the old design.

upwork.title: Payment System
upwork.description: Designed and built a production-style payment platform using Go, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker Compose, and Next.js. The system supports order creation, payment charging, HMAC-secured callbacks, refunds, invoice generation, and transaction logs. Implemented idempotency protection, authorization, transactional outbox processing, retries, dead-letter queues, and background workers for reliable asynchronous workflows.

name: The Gateway
strapline: Next.js BFF over a Go gateway: register upstream APIs, forward calls server-side.
hero_cmd: cd project && docker compose up -d postgres
why: Every internal tool ends up with its own copy of the same upstream credentials. This repo is the counter-example: an upstream API is registered once - identifier, host, path, method, allowed headers and parameters - and every client calls the gateway instead of the upstream.

It is also a deliberate exercise in keeping a token out of the browser. Browser to Next.js BFF to Go service, with the JWT in an httpOnly cookie and the signing secret read per request from system_properties, so no JWT ever reaches browser JavaScript or localStorage.
what: It is a self-hosted API management console: you register an upstream API by giving it an identifier, host, path, method, and the headers or parameters it may pass through, then the gateway forwards those calls for you.

It also manages store accounts (a client id plus a secret key you can regenerate) and keeps the login token in a server-side httpOnly cookie, so no JWT ever reaches browser JavaScript or localStorage.
It is for a developer or small team that wants one controlled front door for internal or third-party APIs instead of scattering upstream credentials across every client app.

stack.name: Next.js 15 + React 19 + TypeScript
stack.role: BFF and console in one app: route handlers and server-side lib code mean the JWT never has to leave the server, and the console is plain app-router pages.

stack.name: Go (chi + pgx)
stack.role: The gateway itself: a small router, one typed store file per entity over pgx, and forwarders with explicit dial and client timeouts.

stack.name: PostgreSQL
stack.role: Users, store accounts, registered APIs, and the system_properties row that holds the signing secret - read per request rather than cached in the process.

stack.name: JWT + httpOnly cookie
stack.role: Auth across the seam: login issues a JWT, the BFF keeps it in a SameSite=Lax httpOnly cookie, and a Bearer middleware in Go guards everything except /health and login.

stack.name: Kubernetes
stack.role: The Go service ships with a Deployment (2 replicas, /health probes, 32Mi request / 64Mi limit) and an HPA that scales 2 to 10 pods on CPU 60% and memory 70%.

structure: frontend/src/app/gw/[...path]/route.ts - the catch-all BFF route; frontend/src/lib/gwRoutes.ts is the declarative route table and frontend/src/lib/bffGateway.ts owns session-to-401 mapping, the 20s AbortController, sanitization and envelope translation.
frontend/src/lib/session.ts and frontend/src/middleware.ts - the httpOnly cookie session and the guard over /home, /api/* and /store/*.
gateway-go/internal/handler/ - chi routes plus the Bearer-token middleware; only /health and /gateway/user/login stay public.
gateway-go/internal/store/ - one file per entity (user, account, api, postgres.go) over pgx.
gateway-go/internal/service/ - forward.go (typed ForwardRequest) and upstream.go (persisted header allowlist, single query encode, 5s dial / 30s client timeout).
k8s/gateway-go/ - deployment.yaml and hpa.yaml.
architecture: All backend calls are server-side: the browser only ever talks to the Next.js BFF, which attaches the JWT from the httpOnly cookie and translates upstream failures into NextResponse envelopes.
The route table is data, not code: gwRoutes.ts declares which gateway paths exist, so adding an upstream surface is an edit in one file - and the current table accepts only GET and POST.
Auth is two-layered: the BFF owns the session cookie, and the Go service re-checks the Bearer token on everything under /api/gateway and /api/store before a handler runs.
Forwarding is allowlisted: upstream.go applies the persisted header and parameter allowlist, encodes the query once, and bounds the call with a 5s dial and 30s client timeout.
Scale-out is declared rather than assumed: the HPA runs 2 to 10 pods, while login throttling is per-username and in memory, so it resets on restart and does not aggregate across replicas.
The Kubernetes manifests cover gateway-go only; the frontend and PostgreSQL run outside the cluster, and the repo publishes no load-test numbers.
install: cd project && docker compose up -d postgres
quickstart: Seed the database with project/pg-init-scripts/gateway.sql: it creates the api_gateway table with three example upstreams pointing at https://api.thecatapi.com.
Start the Go service and the frontend, then open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with a seeded user from that same SQL file.
You land on /home (frontend/src/app/home/page.tsx) with API and Store tabs listing the configured upstreams and store accounts.

Click an API row to open its detail page, edit the allowed headers and parameters, then press Try it Now! to send a real request through /gw/apis/execute/<identifier> and see the upstream response body.
curl http://localhost:8080/health returns {"status":"ok"}, the same check the Kubernetes probes use.
tradeoffs: The README has no limitations section, so the scope notes here are read off the code rather than claimed.
Login throttling is per-username and in memory (gateway-go/internal/auth/auth.go), so counters reset on restart and do not aggregate across the 2 to 10 replicas the HPA can run.
The BFF route table accepts only GET and POST (frontend/src/lib/gwRoutes.ts) even though upstream forwarding itself supports GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
Kubernetes manifests cover gateway-go only (k8s/gateway-go/); the frontend and PostgreSQL have no Deployment or Service, and the repo ships no benchmark or load-test numbers at all.

upwork.title: The Gateway
upwork.description: Built an API gateway platform with a Next.js 15 Backend-for-Frontend layer in front of a Go gateway service and PostgreSQL. The BFF proxies requests server-side, applying auth, timeouts and envelope mapping, and never exposes JWTs to browser JavaScript. The Go gateway implements JWT authentication, rate limiting, API and store services, and forwarding to configured upstream APIs, shipped with Kubernetes manifests.

name: routre
strapline: One static Go binary that cuts AI token bills and fails over providers for any CLI.
why: Agent traffic is repetitive: the same diff, the same grep hits, the same build log are re-sent on every turn and billed again. routre sits on the loopback address between the app and the provider, shrinks that noise before it is billed, and answers identical requests from cache - so a session costs less without the agent changing.

The second motive is availability. Subscription providers get busy or rate-limited mid-task, so the gateway walks provider tiers and fails over instead of failing the request, and keeps a per-agent ledger because nobody could otherwise say what a session actually cost.
what: routre is a small local gateway that sits between your AI apps and AI providers on your own machine. Point a coding agent at http://127.0.0.1:20128 once and it keeps working while routre shrinks repetitive tool output before it is billed, replays identical requests from a cache, and switches to the next provider if one is busy or down.
It ships as one static Go binary (10.9 MiB) with no Node, Python, Postgres or Redis; it idles at about 12.6 MiB RAM, adds ~26 ms p50 on a 1 MiB body, and its bundled catalog lists 509 models.
The shipped RTK level is "routre": the repo's benchmark measures 94.8% aggregate / 93.3% worst-payload tool-token reduction (level: standard measures ~91%).

It is aimed at anyone running OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible CLIs (opencode, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) who wants lower token bills and less downtime, plus a per-agent token/cost ledger and a loopback-only browser dashboard.

stack.name: Go, standard library only
stack.role: One static binary (10.9 MiB, ~12.6 MiB idle) with no Node, Python, Postgres or Redis; the proxy is net/http, so no framework sits between the reader and the request path.

stack.name: HTTP + SSE dialects
stack.role: internal/proxy/dialect/ is a cross-kind SSE state machine (OpenAI to Anthropic to Gemini), which is what lets one address serve every OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible CLI.

stack.name: RTK compression
stack.role: 11 heuristic tool_result filters (git diff and log, grep, tree/ls/find dedup, build output, smart truncate) that never grow a payload and fail open; the shipped level measures 94.8% aggregate tool-token reduction.

stack.name: LRU response cache
stack.role: Exact-match on the SHA-256 of the canonical body after RTK; streaming and non-streaming entries share a key space but never cross, and an on-disk snapshot keeps the cache warm across restarts.

stack.name: Local config + loopback dashboard
stack.role: routre setup writes config.json and routre.env (0600), and the loopback-only /ui edits keys and routing without hand-editing JSON.

structure: main.go plus one file per command - setup.go, start.go, stop.go, list.go, models.go, bench.go, update.go; bench.go is the gate that fails on any RTK regression below the target.
internal/proxy/ - the pipeline with runner.go for retry and failover; internal/proxy/dialect/ holds the cross-kind SSE state machine.
internal/rtk/ - the 11 heuristic tool_result filters, each bounded by a 512 KiB scan window and a 150 ms budget.
internal/cache/ - the exact-match LRU keyed on the SHA-256 of the canonical post-RTK body, with its on-disk snapshot for warm restarts.
internal/router/ - tier walking and per-provider cooldown; internal/usage/ - the ~/.routre/usage.json token and cost ledger.
The loopback-only /ui dashboard is served from internal/proxy/, so the gateway and its settings page ship in the same binary.
architecture: Every request walks the same seven steps: detect dialect, RTK compress, cache lookup, tiered route, candidateRunner retry, translate, relay.
Compression is bounded and fail-open: no filter may enlarge a payload, and the work stops at the scan window or the time budget rather than delaying the request.
Routing prefers the cheapest healthy provider: tiers are walked in config order (subscription, then cheap, then free) and a failure puts that provider on an exponential cooldown from 2s to 5m.

Failover is bounded, not open-ended: one transient retry, one auth refresh on 401/403, then the next candidate; timeouts.candidate_seconds defaults to 45s with one bounded 45s extension and a 120s header ceiling.
The ledger is derived from the path that bills: internal/usage/ records per-agent tokens and cost, including what RTK and the cache saved.
Savings are measured on tool-result tokens only - output tokens are never compressed - so the published percentage is a benchmark instrument, not a billing guarantee.
quickstart: routre setup — wizard writes config.json (providers, tiers, models) and routre.env (API keys, 0600) with no shell exports needed.
routre check — validates the config and reports which API keys are set.
routre serve — starts the gateway on 127.0.0.1:20128 in the foreground (routre start --autostart for a daemon at boot).
curl http://127.0.0.1:20128/healthz — returns ok; then run any agent with OPENAI_BASE_URL/ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointed at the gateway.
routre list — shows connected providers plus the per-agent token and cost ledger, including rtk and cache savings.
Open http://127.0.0.1:20128/ui in a browser to set keys and edit the full config without touching JSON by hand.
tradeoffs: The ≥90% figure is measured on tool-result tokens only; output tokens are never compressed, so real-session savings depend on how tool-heavy your traffic is.
Token estimates are an approximation (≈4 bytes/token) — a benchmark instrument, not billing-grade; tiktoken integration is listed as planned.
The npm distribution is deprecated: the package prints the curl command and exits, and no release automation remains for it.
Windows self-update is deferred — routre update on Windows prints a re-install hint instead of replacing the running .exe; Windows binaries are still shipped for manual install.

upwork.title: routre
upwork.description: Developed a lightweight local LLM gateway for coding agents using Go. The gateway provides a unified interface for multiple providers, automatic failover, model-list refresh, response caching, token compression, and per-agent token and cost tracking. Designed as a low-memory static binary with no external runtime dependencies, improving reliability and visibility for local AI-assisted development workflows.

widgets.title: What happens to one request
widgets.intro: Seven steps run in order. Choose a cache miss to follow a full upstream round-trip, or a cache hit to see where the reply short-circuits.

steps.title: Detect dialect
steps.what: Work out whether the caller is speaking OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini.
steps.detail: The three dialects differ in paths, headers and event shapes. routre normalises the incoming request here so every later step sees one shape.

steps.title: RTK compress
steps.what: Shrink repetitive tool output before it is billed, and fail open if it cannot.
steps.detail: 11 heuristic filters target diffs, logs, grep hits, file trees and build noise. Compression is fail-open and never grows a payload; very large payloads stop at a 512 KiB scan window or a 150 ms budget.

steps.title: Cache lookup
steps.what: Hash the processed body and look for an identical earlier request.
steps.detail: The key is SHA-256 over the canonical JSON body after RTK. On a hit the saved response is replayed byte-for-byte with no upstream call, so the request jumps straight to the relay.

steps.title: Route across tiers
steps.what: Pick the cheapest healthy provider from the subscription → cheap → free tiers.
steps.detail: Tiers are walked in config order and a provider that just failed is held back by an exponential cooldown (2 s to 5 m), so a busy provider is skipped rather than retried forever.

steps.title: Retry / failover
steps.what: Retry once, refresh an expired token, then move to the next provider.
steps.detail: One immediate connection-level retry, one free auth refresh on 401/403, then failover. Each candidate gets an adaptive slice — timeouts.candidate_seconds is 45 s by default, with one bounded 45 s extension while the socket is alive.

steps.title: Translate dialect
steps.what: Rewrite the upstream answer back into the dialect the caller asked for.
steps.detail: A cross-kind SSE state machine converts streaming events on the fly, so an OpenAI-shaped client can talk to an Anthropic provider and vice versa.

steps.title: Relay
steps.what: Stream the answer home — from upstream on a miss, from memory on a hit.
steps.detail: On a miss the upstream stream is relayed as it arrives; on a hit the saved stream is replayed. Mid-stream aborts are never cached.

widgets.title: Get started in 3 steps
widgets.intro: Copy each block and tick it off. Progress is remembered in this browser only.

steps.title: Install the binary
steps.body: Download the latest release and put routre on your PATH. Nothing else is installed.

steps.title: Run setup, then start it
steps.body: The wizard writes config.json (providers, tiers, models) and a 0600 routre.env for your API keys. routre serve starts the gateway on 127.0.0.1:20128.

steps.title: Point your client at the gateway
steps.body: Export the gateway URL for your client, then open the dashboard to add keys. Any OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible CLI now routes through routre.
steps.cmd:
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:20128
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:20128
open http://127.0.0.1:20128/ui

items.q: Does my code leave my machine?
items.a: Only in the prompt you already send to your AI provider, and only to that provider. routre binds to 127.0.0.1, so it is reachable from your own computer and not from the network, and it puts no third party between you and the provider.

items.q: Do I need Node, Python, Postgres or Redis?
items.a: No. routre is one static Go binary. Install it, run routre setup, and it manages its own JSON config, on-disk cache and token ledger. There is no runtime, database or message broker to run.

items.q: What happens if a provider is down or busy?
items.a: routre retries once, refreshes an expired auth token if needed, then moves to the next candidate in tier order. A provider that fails is cooled down for 2 s to 5 m, and the whole attempt stays inside configurable timeouts (a 45 s candidate slice by default).

items.q: Will it work with Claude Code, Codex, opencode or Cursor?
items.a: Yes. Any client that speaks the OpenAI or Anthropic HTTP API works — point OPENAI_BASE_URL or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at http://127.0.0.1:20128. Cross-dialect translation means an OpenAI-shaped client can reach an Anthropic provider and vice versa.
routre itself is MIT-licensed open source with no paid tier. You still pay your AI providers for the tokens you use; RTK compression and the response cache are what cut the tokens billed.

It does not compress output tokens, its token estimates are approximate (~4 bytes/token, a benchmark instrument rather than billing-grade), the npm package is deprecated, and Windows self-update is deferred. It is a local gateway, not a hosted service.

name: Trading Suite
strapline: Self-hosted IDX market desk: FastAPI over a SQLite WAL cache, five UI routes.
why: This repo exists to answer one question once a session: which Indonesian stocks should be bought at the next open, and why. It is a self-hosted desk - your own FastAPI backend, your own cached copy of the market data - instead of another market-data subscription.

The strongest feature is bandarmology, Indonesian broker-flow analysis: phase, intent radar and flow metrics computed from broker activity, with a FIFO portfolio engine and a backtest surface behind the same API, so a number on screen can be traced back to the code that produced it.
what: A self-hosted desk for the Indonesian stock market (IDX). It pulls quotes, history, foreign flow and broker activity from public feeds, caches them, and turns them into five screens: an overview, a charting page with foreign-flow bars, a streaming screener, a per-ticker profiler, and calculators.
It is for one person or a small team who wants their own copy of the market data rather than a subscription, and who is happy to run a backend and a front end on their own machine.
Nothing is stored in a company cloud: quotes live in a local SQLite WAL cache under backend/data/cache.db, and the only outbound calls are to the public data sources.

stack.name: Python + FastAPI
stack.role: The backend: one router per domain (market, screener, validator, intel, analysis, regime, backtest, portfolio, summary, alerts, sentiment) with the analysis kept one level up in service modules.

stack.name: SQLite in WAL mode
stack.role: The cache seam: per-feed TTLs with stale-while-revalidate in backend/data/cache.db, so a screen refresh does not hammer the public feeds.

stack.name: Server-Sent Events
stack.role: The screener streams results from GET /api/screener/scan/stream and the client mirrors the same cache policy in src/lib/cache.ts (memory + sessionStorage).

stack.name: Next.js 16 + React + TypeScript
stack.role: The five UI routes (overview, markets, screener, profiler, calculators) after a lean pass from 22 app routes; the nav is generated from one source in src/lib/apps.ts.

stack.name: curl_cffi + yfinance
stack.role: The data path: an IDX summary endpoint and .JK history - cached copies of third-party feeds, not an exchange-grade tick store, and the repo says so.

structure: backend/app/main.py - wires the routers; backend/app/routers/ holds one router per domain and the services live one level up in backend/app/*.py.
backend/app/screener.py, idx.py, cache.py, db.py - the scan path: the suspended-ticker filter runs before the ThreadPool fan-out, then results stream over SSE from the SQLite WAL cache.
backend/app/validator.py - BandarmologyAnalyzer (phase, intent radar, flow metrics) behind GET /api/validator/{ticker} and inside the profiler page.

backend/app/_fifo.py + portfolio.py - the FIFO P/L engine and its JSON load/save; backend/app/backtest.py + routers/analysis.py - the pattern backtests. Both are API-only: next.config.ts redirects /portfolio and /backtest to /profiler.
frontend src/app/{overview,markets,screener,profiler,calculators} with src/lib/apps.ts as the single nav source, and backend/data/cache.db as the only datastore.
architecture: Caching is the seam that makes it cheap: per-feed TTLs in a SQLite WAL file with stale-while-revalidate and _spawn_refresh dedupe, mirrored in the browser by src/lib/cache.ts.
A scan is filtered before it is fetched: the suspended-ticker filter runs in idx.py before the ThreadPool fans out, so excluded names never reach a feed.
The API is the product surface: routers stay thin and the analysis lives in service modules, so the profiler page, the validator endpoint and the backtest endpoint all read the same engine.
Nothing is stored in a company cloud: quotes live in backend/data/cache.db and the only outbound calls are to the public data sources.
AI summaries are no longer a feature: backend/app/ai.py is an explicit no-op stub that returns None and nothing imports it, so every caller falls back to deterministic text.
quickstart: Start both halves with the runner from the repo root: chmod +x ./trading-suite && ./trading-suite run (backend on :8000, front end on :3000).
Open http://localhost:3000 - the launcher shows exactly five cards: Overview, Markets, Screener, Profiler, Calculators.
Go to /screener: the scan streams in over SSE rather than waiting for one big payload.
Open /profiler?ticker=BBCA - one screen showing quote, candles, beta, regime, the bandarmology phase, the intent radar, the broker panel and an entry plan.
Check the backend directly at http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health, and browse the auto-generated API at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs.
tradeoffs: AI-generated summaries are not a working feature any more: backend/app/ai.py is an explicit no-op stub ('AI section has been dismantled'), it returns None and nothing imports it, so every caller falls back to deterministic text - the README's OPENCODE_GO_API_KEY row is stale and was left out of the claims above.
FIFO portfolio tracking and pattern backtesting are backend-only: next.config.ts hard-redirects /portfolio and /backtest to /profiler, so both show up as API endpoints rather than screens.
Broker data is best-effort and partly credentialed: the Stockbit panel needs STOCKBIT_JWT_TOKEN (or user/password) and shows a degraded message without it.

Accuracy is bounded by third-party sources - an IDX summary endpoint scraped with curl_cffi, yfinance .JK history, and TradingView - so the numbers are cached copies of someone else's feed, not an exchange-grade tick store.

upwork.title: Trading Suite
upwork.description: Built a financial data platform using Python and FastAPI for Indonesian stock market analysis. The platform includes live quotes, multi-ticker screening, technical indicators, bandarmology validation, FIFO portfolio tracking, market-regime filtering, historical backtesting, and AI-generated market summaries. Designed data-processing workflows and API endpoints for market analysis, portfolio calculations, and reproducible trading research.

name: Trading CLI
strapline: Minervini Stage 2 + VCP scanner for ~900 IDX tickers, with 18 backtests and OOS gates.
why: Most screeners answer with a list and no accounting for whether the list makes money. This one answers with a plan and an honest no-trade: roughly 900 IDX tickers screened each morning, then every qualifying pick backtested against 18 strategies with real fees and slippage, tagged with the market regime at entry and re-checked walk-forward out-of-sample.

The output is machine-readable JSON on purpose - picks, near_miss, leaderboard, regime_pooled, wf_regime - so a swing trader or an agent can run it before the open and sit out when the evidence is thin instead of forcing a recommendation.
what: It screens roughly 900 IDX/IHSG tickers each morning against the Minervini Trend Template (8 checks) plus a VCP contraction score, then plans the entry zone, stop and targets for the ones that qualify.

Each pick is also backtested across 18 strategies with real IDX fees and slippage, tagged with the market regime at entry, and re-checked walk-forward out-of-sample so a threshold is only kept when it survives unseen data.
It is for a swing trader or a screening agent that wants machine-readable output and an explicit no-trade answer instead of a forced recommendation.

stack.name: Python 3.11+ and pandas
stack.role: The whole tool is one CLI (trading_cli/cli.py); indicators and scan math are pandas over daily bars - no server, no API keys, no database to run.

stack.name: yfinance + SQLite
stack.role: The data path: a throttled 4-thread fetch with rate-limit backoff over a 12h-TTL WAL cache in the XDG cache directory, with stale-while-revalidate.

stack.name: Minervini Trend Template + VCP
stack.role: The screen itself: 8 trend checks plus a volatility-contraction score, with relative strength measured against ^JKSE before any candidate is planned.

stack.name: Walk-forward validation
stack.role: Rolling train-252 / step-60 windows: a threshold is kept only when it survives unseen data, which is why the README reports roughly 50% pooled win rate instead of a 70% sleeve.

stack.name: Expectancy + Wilson interval
stack.role: Ranking is by expectancy p*avgWin + (1-p)*avgLoss and a 95% Wilson bound, not raw win rate, so a high win rate with 0.5R losers cannot top the leaderboard.

structure: trading_cli/cli.py - the whole surface (the trading-cli script in pyproject.toml): flags, scan, expectancy ranking, qualifiers split from near_miss, JSON out.
trading_cli/scan.py, minervini.py, data.py, cache.py - universe fetch and throttling, trend template, VCP score and relative strength over the SQLite cache.
trading_cli/backtest.py + regime.py - the 18-entry STRATS table, next-open fills with fees and slippage, and the regime tags each trade carries.
trading_cli/validate.py + tune.py - walk-forward out-of-sample replay and the VCP threshold grid under the same gate.
trading_cli/entry.py + ml_filter.py - buy zone, tightest stop and T1/T2/T3 targets, plus the pooled-n and leakage guards that keep future ML work honest.
architecture: One pass produces the answer: scan the universe, gate on regime (ADTV, ATR14, IHSG stage, CMF), rank survivors by expectancy, then split them into qualifiers and near_miss.
Every pick carries its evidence: the strategies that backtested it, the pooled win rate with a Wilson bound, and the regime tag at entry.
Thresholds are earned rather than chosen: validate.py replays strategies on rolling windows and tune.py grids VCP thresholds under the same out-of-sample gate.
The entry plan is derived from the pivot: the 20-day high becomes the buy zone, and the tightest of the 20-day low, close minus 2 ATR or -8% becomes the stop.
Data is daily and best-effort: yfinance with throttle and backoff, so coverage is only as good as that feed - reported in the README rather than hidden.
install: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e .   # requires Python 3.11+, yfinance>=0.2.40, pandas>=2.0, numpy>=1.24
trading-cli --doctor   # probes yfinance and cache health
quickstart: trading-cli --scan-only --limit 50 --period 1y — the fastest run: a qualifier table plus the NEAR MISS block, a few seconds when cached. --scan-only skips the backtest stages, so the 70% HUNT and leaderboard blocks only appear on a full run.
trading-cli --ticker BBCA — one-ticker deep dive with the Trend Template checks, VCP score, entry plan and per-strategy backtest stats.
trading-cli --json > picks.json then jq '.leaderboard' — the machine-readable expectancy leaderboard the agent workflow parses.
trading-cli --period 2y --validate — per-window out-of-sample results for the top strategies plus the pooled wf_regime block.
trading-cli --doctor — confirms the data path with a live probe of ^JKSE plus sample tickers and reports cache size.
tradeoffs: The README's own honesty section states there is no proven 70% win-rate sleeve on daily yfinance OHLCV alone: every higher-R and divergence candidate failed both the pooled Wilson gate and the 2y walk-forward gate, and the measured ceiling is about 50% pooled win.

Institutional and broker-flow filters are not built: broker concentration or a foreign net-buy streak needs an idx.co.id scrape the README calls fragile, so it stays deferred behind ml_filter.gate_pooled_n(need=100), and there is no intraday VWAP because the data path is daily yfinance only.

Regime gating is deliberately soft (a -20 combo demote, not a hard veto) with fixed, untuned thresholds, so Stage 4 tape still produces candidates; changing it is gated on out-of-sample evidence at n>=100.
Everything depends on Yahoo Finance daily data through trading_cli/data.py, which throttles and needs --workers 4 when it answers 401/429, so coverage and quality are only as good as that feed.

upwork.title: Trading CLI
upwork.description: Created a Python command-line stock screening tool for Indonesian and IHSG markets. The application detects Stage 2 trends, volatility contraction patterns, pullbacks, breakouts, and reversals. It also includes technical indicators, institutional-flow analysis, market-regime filters, multiple backtesting strategies, and walk-forward out-of-sample evaluation for more disciplined and reproducible analysis.

name: t-notes
strapline: Local-first notes and kanban in the browser - no cloud, no framework, no build step.
why: t-notes is the answer to using a board and a notes app for things that should never leave the laptop: no account, no sync service, no build step and no framework. All data stays in browser localStorage, and the board and the notes are one system - a note pinned to a list renders as a card in both views.

It also exists to show how small that can be: the entire UI is three static files, the Windows build is a 9.7 MiB Go exe that embeds them, and the Tauri shell adds one Rust command for large-corpus search.
what: t-notes is a single-user notes app and a kanban board in one, with all data kept in your own browser - nothing is sent to a server, and there is no account or sync service.

A note can also be pinned to a board list, and then the same item shows up as a card in both views, so edits stay in sync. Cards carry checklists with progress, due dates, comments, labels, tags and image attachments.
It is for people who want Trello's core without the cloud: run it from static files on any OS with a browser, or on Windows as a small Go exe or a Tauri desktop app.
An optional AI assistant (bring your own key) can summarize, draft checklists and suggest ideas; the key stays local and is never exported.

stack.name: Vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript
stack.role: web/index.html, styles.css and app.js are the entire UI - no framework, no bundler, no npm install; content-visibility: auto keeps long lists cheap and the three themes are plain CSS.

stack.name: localStorage
stack.role: The only datastore: all state lives under the key t-notes-v1 and is written on every mutation, so there is no API client and no server-side session.

stack.name: Go with //go:embed
stack.role: main.go embeds web/ and serves it from a local net/http server, opens the default browser, and self-installs or uninstalls from the same binary.

stack.name: Tauri v2 + Rust
stack.role: The desktop shell: one Rust command (match_notes) for batch substring search with a JS fallback, and an NSIS installer with a launch-on-login plugin.

stack.name: Playwright
stack.role: e2e/t-notes.spec.js (15 tests) runs against system Chromium with a mocked AI endpoint; build-windows.sh cross-compiles the Windows exe and setup exe from Linux.

structure: web/ - the entire front end: index.html, styles.css, app.js and logo.svg, with const K = t-notes-v1 at the top of app.js as the storage key for all state.
main.go - the Go host: //go:embed web/, the local net/http server, browser launch, and the setup/--install and --uninstall paths.
src-tauri/ - the desktop shell: src/main.rs exposes match_notes, and tauri.conf.json sets frontendDist to ../web and bundles the NSIS installer with tauri-plugin-autostart.
e2e/t-notes.spec.js - the Playwright suite, run against system Chromium with a mocked AI endpoint.
build-windows.sh + go.mod - cross-compile the Windows exe and setup exe from Linux.
architecture: One store, two views: notes pinned to a board list render as cards, so the board and the notes view are the same objects and an edit in either is the same write.
Two host paths share one front end: the Go exe acts as a browser launcher (with an /api/startup fallback for the power toggle) and the Tauri app opens its own window and installer.
State is local-first by construction: no sync layer, no account and no multi-device story - the only optional network call is the bring-your-own-key AI request.
The AI assistant keeps the key in the browser and never exports it; summaries, checklists, rewrites and ideas all run against the URL and key the user supplies.
Long lists stay cheap by capping what is rendered (a 50-item window) and letting content-visibility skip off-screen work.
install: python3 -m http.server 8000   # open http://localhost:8000 (Ctrl-C to stop)
cd ..   # the two optional commands below run from the repo root
sh build-windows.sh   # optional: dist/t-notes.exe + dist/t-notes-setup.exe from Linux (needs Go)
npm install && npx tauri dev   # optional: Tauri desktop app on Linux (needs Rust)
quickstart: Run python3 -m http.server 8000 inside t-notes/web and open http://localhost:8000 - the Notes and board UI loads with no build step.
Click + New note, type a title first, and save: the note appears in the Notes list and a toast confirms every action.
Create a column with the New list… box, then add a card and drag it between columns to see the board update.
Pin a note to a board list so it renders as a card too, then click it to open the detail dialog (body, checklist + progress, list picker, image attachments).
Toggle the theme button to cycle light / dark / midnight - the choice persists across reloads.
Use ⤓ to export all data as JSON and ⤒ to restore it, or the ? button for the in-app guide.
tradeoffs: The Windows installer is unsigned: SmartScreen shows an "Unknown publisher" warning and the user must click More info → Run anyway (signing needs a paid cert, skipped for now).
There is no auto-updater yet - new versions are manual downloads from GitHub Releases.
The first install needs internet once for the WebView2 bootstrapper (nearly all Windows 10/11 PCs already have WebView2).
It is single-user and local-only: data lives in browser localStorage, so there is no sync, no sharing and no multi-device story.

upwork.title: t-notes
upwork.description: Built a local-first notes and Kanban application focused on privacy, offline use, and low resource consumption. The application provides note management, task organization, and board-based workflows without requiring a cloud account. Implemented local persistence, a responsive interface, and desktop packaging with Tauri for users who want full control of their data.

name: arness
strapline: Lean local AI coding harness: one binary, CLI + TUI, MCP/LSP, skills, extensions, optimizer.
why: Most harnesses are a hosted runtime with a CLI attached. arness is the opposite: one local binary you own, where the turn loop, the tools, the provider adapter and the optimizer all live in a single TypeScript source tree, and nothing leaves the machine except the provider call you configured.

The optimizer exists because agent sessions are mostly repetition. Prefix ordering, compression, clamping, breakpoints and pruning are applied before the request, and every saving is appended to a ledger - so the number can be checked instead of claimed.
what: arness is a coding agent that runs entirely on your machine as one binary: an interactive TUI and a print mode over the same turn loop, with tools (bash, filesystem, search), skills, an extension API, MCP and LSP capabilities, subagents, memory and a token optimizer.
It is built to stay small. TypeScript is compiled by bun into a single executable, Node 26 is a build-time requirement only, and the sole devDependency is the compiler used for tsc --noEmit.

State is plain files under your config and state directories - arness.json for configuration, one JSONL event log per session, and optimizer.jsonl with one savings row per provider call - so a session can be forked, switched, inspected or deleted with tools you already have.

It is for people who want a local harness they can read and extend: the spec of record lives in the repository (CONTEXT.md, PLAN.md), the suite runs on node --test against committed SSE captures, and every capability states its boundary - including the bash tool, which is not a sandbox.

stack.name: TypeScript on Node 26
stack.role: Erasable syntax only, checked with tsc --noEmit; TypeScript is the only devDependency, so the source carries no build-time framework.

stack.name: bun build --compile
stack.role: One self-contained executable per platform; install.sh and install.ps1 drop it under the user data directory and link a shim onto PATH.

stack.name: node --test
stack.role: The suite runs on the runtime's own test runner with no framework; provider streams are parsed against committed SSE captures, so tests never touch the network.

stack.name: MCP + LSP
stack.role: src/capabilities/ attaches MCP servers and a language server to the session, so context comes from real tools rather than from the loop guessing.

stack.name: JSONL event log + savings ledger
stack.role: One event log per session under the state directory makes /fork and /switch cheap; optimizer.jsonl keeps one savings row per provider call.

structure: src/main.ts - entrypoint and mode selection: interactive TUI, or -p for one turn, print and exit.

src/core/ - config, events and session, the turn loop, system prompt and skills, token accounting and rendering (config.ts, events.ts, session.ts, loop.ts, system-prompt.ts, skills.ts, tokens.ts, render.ts, commands.ts, context.ts).
src/tools/ - the bash, filesystem and search tools plus the registry; src/ext/ - the extension loader, hooks, host and types.
src/capabilities/ - MCP, LSP, subagents, memory, review, search and todo guards.
src/optimizer/ - prefix order, compression, clamp, breakpoints and prune, with report.ts and rtk.ts; src/providers/openai.ts is the provider adapter.
src/tui/ - input, theme and the terminal UI; test/ - node --test suites with committed SSE fixtures; scripts/check-names.mjs guards against foreign harness references.
architecture: One loop, two front ends: the TUI and print mode drive the same turn loop, so a scripted run and an interactive session take an identical path through tools, capability hooks and the optimizer.
The optimizer runs before the request: it rewrites the outgoing payload and appends a savings row per provider call, which is what makes the ledger auditable.
Sessions are files: every event is appended to sessions/<cwd-slug>/<iso>_<id>.jsonl, so forking, switching and inspecting a session need no database.
Extensions hook the loop: src/ext/ exposes lifecycle hooks, and a tool_call hook can veto a call before it runs, so policy can be added without editing core.
Capabilities are attached, not baked in: MCP servers, a language server, subagents and memory are registered onto the session, which keeps the loop small and the surface testable.
Boundaries are stated rather than implied: the bash tool is unrestricted code execution with no isolation layer, and the extension hook is the intended place to add policy.
quickstart: Install, then run arness with no arguments for an interactive TUI session; arness -p "..." runs one turn, prints the answer to stdout and exits.
Configuration is optional: every key in ~/.config/arness/arness.json has a default, and ARNESS_MODEL, ARNESS_BASE_URL and ARNESS_API_KEY override it for one shell.
Ask for the optimizer report before spending anything: --dry-run prints what would be sent and sends no request.
Read the state directory when a session surprises you: one JSONL event log per session plus optimizer.jsonl with one savings row per provider call.
Check the tree before trusting it: node --run check (no foreign harness references), node --run typecheck, node --run test, or node --run verify for all three in order.
tradeoffs: The bash tool runs bash -lc on Linux/macOS and cmd /c on Windows: unrestricted code execution. This is a single-user local CLI, not a sandbox - there is no isolation layer and none is promised; the tool_call extension hook exists so an extension can veto a call before it runs.
Development needs Node 26 and bun for the compile step. Released binaries are self-contained, but the package version is still 0.0.0 and no benchmark numbers are published.
The repository carries plan documents (MCP-PLAN.md, LSP-PLAN.md, TUI-PLAN.md, EXT-PLAN.md); what is actually built is listed in the README notes, and not every planned item has shipped.
There is no cloud sync, no team surface and no remote execution: state is local files, so a session lives on one machine.

upwork.title: arness
upwork.description: Built a lean local AI coding harness in TypeScript: a single binary with an interactive TUI and a print mode over one turn loop. It ships tools (bash, filesystem, search), an extension API, MCP and LSP capabilities, skills, subagents and memory, plus a token optimizer that orders prefixes, compresses, clamps, prunes and writes a savings ledger. Sessions are plain JSONL event logs and the test suite runs on node --test against committed SSE captures with no network access.
deliverables: Turn loop with tools and skills
